newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEMSA Q4 outshines even best forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FEMSA Q4 outshines even best forecasts.

text.p: Mexican bottler Fomento Economico Mexicano SA de CV (FEMSA) delivered an outstanding fourth quarter, surpassing even the most optimistic market forecasts, analysts said on Friday.
One analyst even boldly predicted that FEMSA's flagship brewery unit could supplant Grupo Modelo as Mexico's top producer in the beer market.

"Outstanding," Bear Stearns analyst Carlos Laboy told Reuters when asked for his first impressions. "There is strength in every single one of the operating divisions. The operating profits are a year ahead of what we thought they would be, and we've been optimistic."

FEMSA reported late Thursday that its 1996 net profit shot to 1.55 billion pesos from a pallid 268 million pesos in 1995. Earnings per share were 2.863 pesos compared to 0.495 a year earlier. A Reuters survey of three industry analysts had forecast 1996 earnings per share of 2.64 pesos.
Results for 1996 sparkled in part because 1995 was a disastrous year due to Mexico's economic crisis.

Operating income jumped 78 percent in the fourth quarter to 667 million peosos on revenue growth of 16 percent to 5.199 billion pesos. Its fourth quarter operating margin was 9.7 percent, up from 7.5 percent in 1995 and a full percentage point higher than most predictions.

"They (the results) were better than expected because they (FEMSA) were able to keep their operating costs down, which really helped the operating margin," said Thomas Mobille, a Latin American beer analyst for Robert Fleming based in Brazil.

The results followed FEMSA's decision Monday to raise beer prices to retailers by 22 percent. The hike is expected to be the first real price increase in several years as Mexican inflation is seen running at about 18 percent this year. The new prices were extremely well-received by analysts.

Laboy said FEMSA is Bear Stearns' only buy-rated Latin American beverage companies, and he sees a 25 percent to 40 percent upside on its stock price, even though FEMSA stock had jumped to 33.20 pesos by at midday Friday from 27.05 on February 13.
"I think FEMSA is on track to become the dominant brewer in Mexico in the next five years," Laboy said.
Right now, Femsa is just behind market-leader Modelo. Femsa has about 45 percent of Mexico's beer sales, with Modelo at around 55 percent.

But few can dispute FEMSA's success in the fourth quarter, when its beer sales volumes grew by 7.2 percent over the fourth quarter of 1995. Modelo's sales volumes grew by 6.6 percent in the same time period.
"I am very impressed (with the FEMSA results)," Greg Rianhard of D.A. Campbell in Los Angeles told Reuters. "I think I was pretty aggressive on my estimates and they surpassed them."
Analysts also were cheered by FEMSA's subsidiary Coca-Cola FEMSA, also known as KOF, which bottles and distributes the world's most famous soft drink in Mexico and Argentina.
They said they were particularly impressed with KOF's performance in Argentina, where KOF posted an 11.9 percent profit margin in the fourth quarter after losing money earlier in the year.
Morevover, in Mexico, KOF now has higher operating profit margins in nominal dollar terms than before the devastating peso devaluation of December 1994, Laboy said.
"Not too many companies in Mexico can say that," Laboy said.
